hmmt-feb-2016-geo-01.title: The polygon is a plus sign
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-01.body:
The interior angles sum to $10\cdot180^\circ=1800^\circ$; with $u$ right angles and $12-u$ reflex ones, $90u+270(12-u)=1800$ gives $u=8$: eight convex and four reflex vertices. Since all sides are $2$ and axis-parallel, the polygon is the boundary of a union of $2\times2$ squares in which every maximal boundary segment is a single square side; the only such shape is the plus sign made of $5$ squares (area $20$). Put it at $(2,0),(4,0),(4,2),(6,2),(6,4),(4,4),(4,6),(2,6),(2,4),(0,4),(0,2),(2,2)$ (the four reflex vertices are $(4,2),(4,4),(2,4),(2,2)$).

The letters $Q,W,A,R,T,Z,S,P,H,I,N,X$ go around the polygon in either direction starting at any vertex, so $S,I,X$ are the vertices at cyclic offsets $6,9,11$ from $Q$. Checking all $12$ starting vertices (the other direction gives mirror images): if $Q$ is a reflex vertex the area is $2$ (e.g. $Q=(4,2)$: $S=(2,4)$, $I=(2,2)$, $X=(4,0)$, area $\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2$); otherwise it is $6$ (e.g. $Q=(2,0)$: $S=(4,6)$, $I=(0,4)$, $X=(2,2)$, area $\frac12|{-4}\cdot(-4)-(-2)(-2)|=6$).

**Answer: $2$ or $6$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-02.title: Reflect the circumcenter
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-02.body:
The reflection of $H$ over $AB$ lies on the circumcircle of $ABC$, so the circumcircle of $AHB$ is the reflection of the circumcircle of $ABC$ over $AB$; its centre is the reflection $O_C$ of the circumcenter $O$ over $AB$. Likewise the circumcenter of $AHC$ is the reflection $O_B$ of $O$ over $AC$. The foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ is the midpoint $M_C$ of $AB$, so $O_C=2M_C-O$ and similarly $O_B=2M_B-O$. Then $O_BO_C=2M_BM_C=2\cdot\frac{BC}2=BC=14$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-03.title: Symmetry
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-03.body:
The inradius of $T$ is $\frac5{2\sqrt3}\approx1.44<2<$ circumradius $\frac5{\sqrt3}\approx2.89$, so each corner of $T$ sticks out of $\omega$ (a shaded region, area $X$) and $\omega$ sticks out of $T$ across each side (a starred region, area $Y$); by symmetry there are three of each. Then $[T]=[T\cap\omega]+3X$ and $[\omega]=[T\cap\omega]+3Y$, so $[T]-[\omega]=3(X-Y)$ and $$X-Y=\frac{[T]-[\omega]}3=\frac{\frac{25\sqrt3}4-4\pi}3=\frac{25\sqrt3}{12}-\frac{4\pi}3.$$

**Answer: $\frac{25\sqrt3}{12}-\frac{4\pi}{3}$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-04.title: $D$ is the circumcenter
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-04.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $ABC$. Since $\angle AMO=\angle ANO=90^\circ$, $O$ lies on the circle with diameter $AO$, which is the circumcircle of $AMN$. Also $\angle ATB=2\angle C$ (exterior angle of the isosceles triangle $ATC$) and $\angle AOB=2\angle C$, so $O$ lies on the circumcircle of $BAT$. Hence the second intersection point is $D=O$ and $DC=R$, the circumradius of $ABC$. By Heron, $[ABC]=\sqrt{9\cdot6\cdot1\cdot2}=6\sqrt3$, so $R=\frac{3\cdot8\cdot7}{4\cdot6\sqrt3}=\frac7{\sqrt3}=\frac{7\sqrt3}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-05.title: Radical axes and radical centres
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-05.body:
The lines are the radical axes of the pairs of circles. Among $36$ distinct lines there are $\binom{36}2=630$ pairs. Three circles with non-collinear centres have concurrent pairwise radical axes (the radical centre); this happens for each of the $\binom93=84$ triples, and in each case three pairs of lines meet at one point instead of three distinct points, a loss of $2$ points. Otherwise, in generic position, no two radical axes are parallel and no further coincidences occur (the circles can be chosen so). So the maximum number of intersection points is $630-2\cdot84=462$.

**Answer: 462**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-06.title: Height $AK$ and base $UV$
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-06.body:
By the law of cosines $BC^2=25+64-40=49$, $BC=7$. Let $AI$ meet $EF$ at $K$ and $\Gamma$ again at $Y$ (the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$). Then $XY$ is a diameter, so $\angle XAY=90^\circ$ and $AX\perp AI$; also $EF\perp AI$ (as $AE=AF$). Hence $AX\parallel EF$ and the distance from $X$ to line $UV=EF$ is $AK$.

$AE=AF=\frac{AB+AC-BC}2=3$ and $\angle A=60^\circ$, so $AEF$ is equilateral and $AK=3\cos30^\circ=\frac{3\sqrt3}2$.

Since $MN\parallel AB$ and $MP\parallel AC$, the triangles $MVU$, $FPV$ (and $UEN$) are equilateral. $PF=AF-AP=3-\frac52=\frac12$, so $PV=\frac12$, and $UV=MV=MP-PV=\frac{AC}2-\frac12=\frac72$. Therefore $[XUV]=\frac12\cdot UV\cdot AK=\frac12\cdot\frac72\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}2=\frac{21\sqrt3}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{21\sqrt3}{8}$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-07.title: Thales' theorem holds mod $p$
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-07.body:
$\vec{AB}=(-3,1)$ and $\vec{AC}=(2,6)$ have dot product $-6+6=0$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ (it exists mod $2017$ since $2$ is invertible). For any $A$: $|A-M|^2=\frac{|(A-B)+(A-C)|^2}4=\frac{|A-B|^2+|A-C|^2+2(A-B)\cdot(A-C)}4=\frac{|BC|^2}4$ when the dot product is $0$, and $|B-M|^2=|C-M|^2=\frac{|BC|^2}4$ too. So $O=M$ is equidistant from $A,B,C$, and $d_{2017}(O,A)=\frac{|BC|^2}4=\frac{5^2+5^2}4=\frac{25}2\equiv25\cdot1009=25225\equiv1021\pmod{2017}$.

**Answer: 1021**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-08.title: Probability that a point is swallowed by its neighbours
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-08.body:
The six rays are $60^\circ$ apart, so the origin is inside the hull, and $P_i$ fails to be a vertex iff it lies in triangle $OP_{i-1}P_{i+1}$ (only the segment $P_{i-1}P_{i+1}$ can cross ray $l_i$ farther out). Let $|P_{i-1}|=a$, $|P_{i+1}|=b$ ($\angle P_{i-1}OP_{i+1}=120^\circ$, bisected by $l_i$). The segment $P_{i-1}P_{i+1}$ meets $l_i$ at distance $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ from $O$ (angle-bisector length: $\frac{2ab\cos60^\circ}{a+b}$). So $P_i$ is swallowed with probability $$p=E\left[\frac{ab}{a+b}\right]=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{ab}{a+b}\,da\,db=2\int_0^1a^2\,da\int_0^1\frac t{1+t}\,dt=\frac23(1-\ln2)$$ (using the symmetry $a\ge b$ and $b=at$). By linearity, $E[n]=6(1-p)=6-4(1-\ln2)=2+4\ln2$.

**Answer: $2+4\ln2$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-09.title: Euler's formula and Stewart's theorem
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-09.body:
Let $O,R$ be the circumcenter and circumradius. Since $AB=AD$, $A$ is the midpoint of arc $BD$ not containing $C$, so $AO\perp BD$, $I\in AO$, and $A,J,C$ are collinear (bisector of $\angle BCD$) with $AJ=AB=49$ (incenter–excenter lemma), $JC=73-49=24$. $BD$ bisects $IJ$, so $I,J$ are at the same distance $r$ from $BD$: both triangles have inradius $r$. By Euler's formula $OI^2=R(R-2r)=OJ^2=:x^2$. Power of the point $J$: $R^2-x^2=AJ\cdot JC=1176$, and $R^2-x^2=2Rr$, so $2Rr=1176$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $IJ$ (on $BD$) and $K=AO\cap BD$. As $OI=OJ$, $OM\perp IJ$, so $\triangle IMO\sim\triangle IKM$ (both right, sharing $\angle I$) and $IM^2=IK\cdot IO=rx$, i.e. $IJ^2=4rx$.

Stewart's theorem in $\triangle AOJ$ with cevian $JI$ ($AI=R-x$, $IO=x$): $49^2x+x^2(R-x)=R\left(4rx+x(R-x)\right)$, which simplifies to $(R-x)^2=49^2-4Rr=2401-2352=49$, so $R-x=7$. Then $R+x=\frac{R^2-x^2}{R-x}=168$, so $R=\frac{175}2$, $x=\frac{161}2$, $r=\frac{1176}{2R}=\frac{168}{25}$. Finally $IJ=2\sqrt{rx}=2\sqrt{\frac{168}{25}\cdot\frac{161}2}=\frac25\sqrt{13524}=\frac{28\sqrt{69}}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{28\sqrt{69}}{5}$**

hmmt-feb-2016-geo-10.title: Radical axis of the two mixtilinear incircles
hmmt-feb-2016-geo-10.body:
Let $I$ be the incenter, $\gamma$ the incircle, $I_A$ the $A$-excenter, $M$ the midpoint of arc $BC$ (not containing $A$), and $N$ the midpoint of $ID$. Facts: $M$ has equal power ($MB_2^2=MC_2^2=MB_1\cdot MT_B$, where the mixtilinear circles touch $BC$ at $B_2,C_2$ and $\Gamma$ at $T_B,T_C$) with respect to both mixtilinear incircles, and $N$ is the radical centre of $\omega_B,\omega_C,\gamma$ (because $I$ is the midpoint of $B_1B_2$ and of $C_1C_2$, so the radical axis of $\omega_B$ and $\gamma$ passes through the midpoints of their common tangents). Hence the radical axis of $\omega_B,\omega_C$ is line $MN$, which is perpendicular to $O_BO_C$. So $DH\parallel MN$.

A homothety at $I$ with ratio $2$ sends $M\mapsto I_A$ (as $M$ is the midpoint of $II_A$) and $N\mapsto D$, so $MN\parallel DI_A$. Thus $D,H,I_A$ are collinear. A homothety at $D$ then shows this happens exactly when $H$ is the midpoint of the altitude from $A$.

Let $a=BC$, $b=2$, $c=\sqrt3$ and $S_A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}2$ etc. The orthocenter has barycentric coordinates $(S_BS_C:S_CS_A:S_AS_B)$; $H$ lies on the $A$-midline iff $S_BS_C=S_A(S_B+S_C)=a^2S_A$. With $S_A=\frac{7-a^2}2$, $S_B=\frac{a^2-1}2$, $S_C=\frac{a^2+1}2$ this reads $\frac{a^4-1}4=\frac{a^2(7-a^2)}2$, i.e. $3a^4-14a^2-1=0$, so $a^2=\frac{7+2\sqrt{13}}3$ (positive root).

**Answer: $BC=\sqrt{\frac{7+2\sqrt{13}}{3}}$**
